items.title: A development runtime for native programs: run them without the Rust toolchain in the loop, swap changed modules while state survives, so change-to-seen is near instant (the owner's idea: a 1:1 interpreter)
items.kind: design (native development loop; the owner's proposal; paper + spike before any build)
items.discussion: the owner, 2026-11-17, answering MAP.md section 13.3: 'Improving compilation speed benefits development specifically. Release builds can be much slower ... Development can usually sacrifice execution speed for DX wins. Thus, perhaps a 1:1 interpreter would address this? Modules can be swapped on the fly while preserving state/memory.'
items.area: crates/vilan-core (transformer.rs, interpreter.rs), crates/vilan-cli (hmr.rs, the run command), crates/vilan-rt-gfx/src/host, vilan/std/src/gfx.vl + ui.vl (the `__gfx_*` / `__ui_*` externs)
items.body: The idea separates the two jobs the Rust backend does today: release builds (slow is fine, rustc and LLVM stay) and the development loop (speed of change matters, run-time speed does not). THREE DOORS, the integrator's reading, none measured: (A) THE JS BACKEND IS ALREADY THAT INTERPRETER. Vilan has a second backend whose semantics the native differential holds equal to the native one on ~95% of the corpus, with an engine (V8) far faster than a tree walker, and a hot-module path that already preserves state for web programs (`vilan run --watch`, hmr.rs, std::web::dev). A server or CLI program can be developed on node today and built natively only for release. What is missing is the same for a GPU UI program, which is native-only because its host is: `std::gfx` and `std::ui` reach `vilan-rt-gfx` through a narrow set of about 85 host functions. Give the JS emission that host, either as a node native addon over `vilan-rt-gfx`'s host API, or by embedding a JS engine in a `vilan dev` host binary that owns the window, and a UI edit becomes a module swap in a running window. The hard parts: one event loop (winit wants the main thread and the loop; node has its own), handles and callbacks across the boundary, and what state survives a swap (the reactive graph and owners: hmr.md's rules for the DOM twin are the precedent). (B) GROW THE CONST INTERPRETER (`interpreter.rs`, 4,471 lines, runs const evaluation today) into a whole-program one: async, every host binding, the reactive runtime. It is a THIRD execution of the language to hold in parity, and a tree walker is slow where debug rendering is already 5 to 10 times slower than release. (C) A bytecode VM of our own: (B)'s cost plus a compiler to bytecode, for speed V8 already gives. Recommendation: a short paper and a spike of (A): the `ui-counter` example drawn by `vilan-rt-gfx` and driven by its JS emission, one module swapped while the counter keeps its value, with the time from save to pixels measured. That answers whether the loop and the boundary work before anything is designed around them. It also bears on F167's open ruling about optimising the GPU stack in the debug profile, and on MAP.md 13.2: a dev runtime removes the per-project cold build from the loop entirely, so the compile-time levers then matter for release and CI only.

items.title: The editor feels spongy on Kolt: a plan for the language server's latency, in order (measure today's Kolt; M194; the solve per keystroke; the unbuilt speed half of `auto` annotations; caches)
items.kind: performance (LSP latency; the owner's priority 2026-11-17; an arc with its own measurements)
items.discussion: the owner, 2026-11-17: 'I really want to consider ways to speed up the language server. Incremental analysis completed, caching more efficiently, and perhaps novel solutions (the `auto` type pinning we talked about a while ago) might be all we need to address the spongey-ness I feel when working on large Vilan projects (Kolt).' State in MAP.md section 4 and survey 04
items.area: crates/vilan-lsp, crates/vilan-core/src/analyzer.rs (the checks phase, resolve_world), analyzer/auto_annotations.rs, incremental.rs, scripts/lsp-latency.py; M110, M194, M79, M140, M19, E297, E121, N208; proposal/auto-annotations.md §9 and §13 (S5)
items.body: WHAT IS MEASURED: a leaf keystroke on the perf exhibit costs 1,090 ms of CPU to diagnostics (mandate 500), css 1,220 ms, a parse break 1,930 ms, flat since v0.54. WHAT IS NOT: the exhibit is a frozen Kolt from BEFORE its reorganisation (N208); today's Kolt is 161 files and 85,048 lines and has never been through the latency harness, so the figure the owner feels is unknown. Hover, completion and colouring do not type-check and should be instant; if those feel slow too, that is a separate defect to look for (the keystroke path's <10 ms figures are printed by the harness and not carried into any report). THE PLAN, in order: (1) MEASURE TODAY'S KOLT: migrate the harness to the new layout (N208), record the six E121 rows plus the keystroke-path latencies, and take one instruction profile of a leaf keystroke split by phase and pass, so the order below is decided by numbers. (2) M194: derived bodies are never filed, so every checking pass sweeps about 126,000 always-live entities per keystroke; the named next lever, and the same item unparks the lens (A185 S3b). (3) THE SOLVE: `resolve_world` runs per keystroke and its constraint fixpoint is 79 to 96% of that pass (M73, M79); a paper first. (4) `auto` ANNOTATIONS, THE SPEED HALF. B570 shipped S0 to S4 in Order 49: the syntax, stale refused with `--fix`, the editor's on-save rewrite, the `[check] auto = "exported"` opt-in. Its S5, 'M110 S6 reads syntactic interfaces for annotated items', has no record of landing and no trace in `incremental.rs`, `item_records.rs` or `id_windows.rs` (grep 2026-11-17; not read closely enough to be certain). That slice is what turns an annotation into speed: an exported item's interface becomes a function of the PARSE, so 'interface unchanged' is known before the edited module is walked, importers are reused without waiting, and a half-typed body no longer moves the interface (paper §9.2: 10% of a recorded Kolt session's keystrokes re-walked 12 modules for that reason; 57% of the owner's body edits were in functions with an inferred return). And Kolt has not opted in: 4 `: auto` sites, no `[check] auto` in its manifest; the paper counted 54 exported annotations the opt-in would write. So: build S5, then opt Kolt in and measure both steps. (5) CACHES: the base-cache budget of 192 MiB no longer holds two Kolt worlds at about 74 MB each (M140); an unchanged package module is re-analysed per round (M19). (6) WHAT TO PROMISE while an analysis runs: publish the edited item's diagnostics first (E297, an owner question). Each step lands with its row re-measured on the SAME exhibit; the mandate row stays the arc's test.

items.title: The GPU UI has never run on a real GPU, on Windows or on macOS: a hardware run kit (a report switch in the host, a probe checklist, a runbook) for the owner's machines
items.discussion: MAP.md sections 8 and 14 item 5; the owner, 2026-11-17: 'just let me know when you're ready. My Windows and macOS machines are available'; native-ui.md §11.7 wrote out a Windows run that no record shows was done
items.area: crates/vilan-rt-gfx (host, gpu.rs, window.rs), vilan/examples/{gfx,ui-counter,ui-todo,ui-notes,ui-virtual-list,ui-icons}, F178 (accessibility verification), F167
items.body: Everything in the GPU stack has been verified on one target: Linux, X11, Mesa's software Vulkan, under a virtual display. Windows is cross-linted and never run; macOS is not even type-checked. THE KIT (lane hw-58, 2026-11-17): (1) a report switch in the host (an environment variable, no std surface): at start, the adapter's name, vendor, device type, backend and driver, the surface format and present mode, the window's scale factor and size; at exit, frame count and the distribution of per-frame CPU time (layout, paint, encode, submit) and of the interval between presented frames; (2) macOS type-checked from Linux if the target can be added, so compile errors are found here; (3) a runbook: prerequisites per system, the exact commands from a checkout of `next`, the six examples in order, what to try in each (resize by dragging, move between monitors of different scale, typing with an input method, sleep and wake, a screen reader: Narrator, VoiceOver), and what to send back (the report text, a screenshot per example at each scale, anything that looked wrong). WHAT THE RUN DECIDES: whether the three back ends wgpu picks (DX12, Metal, Vulkan) draw what the software renderer draws; real frame times; whether the debug profile is usable or F167's dev-profile ruling is urgent; which of IME, focus scopes and a second window a real app meets first.
